steps.telnet: Open the device's admin page and turn Telnet off; if it has no such switch, update its firmware. On the router, delete any port forwarding rule for port 23.
steps.ftp: Turn FTP off on the device, or use SFTP instead. On the router, delete any port forwarding rule for port 21.
steps.smb: Turn file sharing (SMB) off on the device if nobody uses it, or allow only accounts with passwords. On the router, delete any port forwarding rule for ports 139 and 445.
steps.rdp: Turn Remote Desktop (RDP) off on the computer if nobody uses it, or require Network Level Authentication. On the router, delete any port forwarding rule for port 3389.
steps.vnc: Turn screen sharing (VNC) off if nobody uses it, or set a strong password. On the router, delete any port forwarding rule for port 5900.
steps.admin: Change the admin page's default password and update the device's firmware. On the router, delete any port forwarding rule for this port.
steps.unknown: Open each new device on the map and answer "Who is this?". A device you cannot place: block its MAC address on the router and change the Wi-Fi password.
steps.wifi: On the router's admin page, set the Wi-Fi security mode to WPA3 (or WPA2 if a device cannot use WPA3) and set a new Wi-Fi password.
steps.wpa3: On the router's admin page, set the Wi-Fi security mode to WPA3, or WPA2/WPA3, if every device supports it.
steps.unchecked: Check the ports of each device you want to know about; you are asked before each one.

explain.fixed: The brain is not available, so here is the plugin's own explanation.

glossary.title: Terms
help.ipAddress: The number a device has on this network, such as 192.168.0.23. The router hands it out and it can change.
help.macAddress: The hardware address of a device's network adapter, six pairs of hex digits. It stays the same unless the device makes up a random one.
help.manufacturer: Who made the network adapter, read from the first half of the MAC address (the IEEE OUI registry).
help.port: The number a service on a device listens on, such as 23 for Telnet or 443 for HTTPS. An open port means a program answers there.
help.wifiChannel: The slice of radio frequencies a Wi-Fi network sends on. Networks on the same or overlapping channels slow each other down.
help.ping: How long a short message takes to reach a device and come back, in milliseconds. Below 20 ms is fast; above 100 ms is slow.
help.securityMode: How a Wi-Fi network encrypts its traffic and checks its password: WPA3 is the strongest, WEP and an open network the weakest.
help.mdns: The name a device announces on the local network (Bonjour), such as Studio-iMac.local.
help.randomMac: Phones and laptops make up a different MAC address for each Wi-Fi network to be harder to track, so it names no manufacturer.
help.router: The box that connects this network to the internet and hands out IP addresses (the default gateway).
help.congestion: How many networks share a channel and how loud they are. The busier the channel, the slower Wi-Fi gets.
help.signal: How strongly this computer hears the Wi-Fi, in dBm: −50 is strong, −70 weak. Noise is the background hiss.
help.kind: What sort of device it is. The plugin guesses from the manufacturer, the mDNS name and the open ports until you say.
